A message that starts with `/skill:name` runs that skill, as in pi: the request carries the skill's instructions in a note after the text (`appendSkillContext`), which the transcript leaves out, so every agent follows it without looking it up. Pi gets the enabled skills the model may load, with their text files, in its session configuration (`skills/harness.ts`), and its harness writes them into Pi's own skills folder; files past a 384 KB budget, counted in UTF-8 bytes, are left out so the configuration stays inside the harness protocol's line limit. ACP agents keep their own skills.

## References

Messages name layers, pages, and skills with Markdown links in the `openpencil:` scheme, `[Hero](openpencil://node/12:34)` (`chat/references/link.ts`), in both directions: the composer inserts them and the system prompt asks the model to cite what it touched the same way. The composer is a CodeMirror field (`components/chat/composer/`), built like the variable formula field: `@` completes layers (the current page's first, then other loaded pages'), pages, and skills (`references/candidates.ts`), and `/` at the start of a message completes the chat's own commands such as `/compact` and the skills the user can run, or an ACP agent's own commands from `available_commands_update` (`agents/acp/commands.ts`). A chosen command is a reference too, of the `command` kind (`references/command.ts`): the chat reads `/compact` and `/skill:` from the link at the message's start (`leadingCommand`), never by matching typed text, and agents and models get it written out (`commandsAsText`). Typing a command's whole name then a space picks it from the open list, so it becomes the same chip. A reference shows as a chip that edits as one unit. The transcript renders the same chip (`ChatReferenceChip`): replies get references rewritten to an inline `chat-reference` component before Markdown renders them, so other links keep the renderer's own handling, and the user's text is split around them. The selection button inserts the selected layers as references, and the layers a message mentions go with it as previews (`references/nodes.ts`), rebuilt from the text when a sent message is edited, which also runs a `/skill:` again; a message with images still cannot be edited. Hovering a layer chip outlines the layer on the canvas. A chip follows renames, shows its written label once its target is gone, and on click shows the layer on its page, switches to the page, or opens the skill in Settings › Skills; a conversation from another document resolves nothing by ID.

## Messages while the agent works

The field stays open while a reply runs, as in pi and Claude Code (`chat/queue.ts`). Enter queues a steering message and Alt+Enter a follow-up; both show dimmed after the reply until sent. The built-in chat's tool loop also stops once the current step's tool calls finish whenever a steering message waits (`yieldWhen` in `transports/tool-loop.ts`), so that message goes in with the step's results, without the step-limit notice. When a reply ends, steering messages go first, then follow-ups, one per reply; a failed reply keeps them. ACP agents and Pi cannot take a message mid-turn, so theirs wait until the turn ends. Escape, or Stop, ends the reply and sends what waits; Up on the first line takes the waiting messages back into the field, images included; changing conversations drops them.

## A run

`transports/tool-loop.ts` starts a run (`reply/run.ts`) when the message is sent, before the model is reached, so a Stop at any point ends a run that exists. A `Run` belongs to one reply and holds:

* the page it works on, which your navigation does not move and the agent's `switch_page` does;
* the step budget captured when the message started;
* each page as it was before the run first edited it, for `diff_changes`;
* every undo entry its calls pushed, with the tool and call that pushed it;
* the calls that changed the document, and the undone calls it already told the model about.

The chat's agent is one presence entry per document (`presence/registry.ts`). It shows as thinking when the run starts and points at the layers each call changed, on whichever page they are. With Follow agents on, following starts with the run and ends when the agent rests and none of your other agents is at work. An agent you chose to follow keeps you with it while it rests.

## A tool call

Every call of an OpenPencil tool, from the chat, a coding agent through MCP, or WebMCP, runs through `runEditorTool` (`tools/runner.ts`); `tools/index.ts` passes the chat's calls with their reply:

* Calls that change a document take its lock in turn, since whole-page snapshots must not interleave. A reply's call that gets the lock after the reply ended changes nothing and returns an error.
* The document change is captured and pushed as one undo step. A reply's call labels it `aiUndoLabel(tool)` and records it on the call's own run, the one it started in, even if a later reply has begun; another client's call is labelled by its source, such as `Agent` or `WebMCP`.
* The change is recorded for the chat's change review, and the agent points at it.
* A call's result reaches the model as JSON. `eval` converts what a script returns, as MCP and the CLI print it.
* If you undid or redid the run's own edits since the model last heard, the result carries an `undoNote` saying so.

## Images a tool returns

An image a call returns, such as `export_image`'s, reaches the model as a file, and every request sends the whole conversation again. On a connection whose provider documents WebP input itself (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, and DeepSeek: `webpImages` in `providers/registry.ts`, each beside its documentation link), a PNG goes as WebP at quality 90 (`tools/model-image.ts`), unless the WebP comes out larger, as it can for flat renders.

* Measured at the 1280 px default edge on design renders: flat UI is 14–20 KB as PNG and barely smaller as WebP; renders with imagery are 197–289 KB as PNG and 61–86 KB as WebP, at SSIM 0.984–0.995 against the PNG, with small text as legible.
* Only a provider's own documentation counts. An Anthropic- or OpenAI-compatible endpoint, OpenRouter, Z.ai, MiniMax, ChatGPT sign-in, and Cloud may forward to a model server that cannot decode WebP (llama.cpp's server reads images with stb\_image, which has none), so they get PNG.
* JPEG is never chosen for the model: our export paints transparent pixels black.
* Core's adapter encodes the image as each request is built (`encodeModelImage` in `tools/ai-adapter.ts`), once per tool call, and the result keeps the tool's PNG, so a conversation continued on a PNG-only connection still sends PNG.
* The app loads CanvasKit's full build, which encodes WebP and JPEG, because a WebView cannot be relied on: WKWebView answers a canvas asked for WebP with PNG.
* Chat Completions takes only text in a tool message, and the AI SDK sends a tool's image there as its Base64 text. On the connections that use it (MiniMax, Cloud, and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint set to Chat Completions), `providers/tool-images.ts` moves each image into a user message after the step's tool results, as opencode does. The same history always gives the same messages, so cached prefixes still match.

## A reply ends

A run ends once, in one of three ways: finished (`onFinish`), failed (`handleError`), or stopped (the request's abort signal). The agent goes idle and its cursor leaves the canvas. A tool already running keeps going: its edit lands in its run, but cannot move the agent again.

When the chat's own `onFinish` reports a reply that was stopped, failed, or cut off, `settleEndedReply` waits for the run's last edit, then settles the message (`reply/settle.ts`):

* reasoning and text are marked done;
* each call that never reported back fails with whether it changed the document, which the model reads next time;
* a stopped reply is marked stopped.

Diagnostics record `chat.completed`, `chat.stopped`, or `chat.failed`.

A reply that finished or failed on its own, rather than one you stopped or one cut off by a disconnect, also reaches `notifyReplyEnded` (`chat/notifications.ts`). It quotes the last text part as plain text and sends it through the shared notification service (`shell/notifications/`), which sends nothing while you are looking at that document. An ACP agent's permission request that is still unanswered after `AGENT_INPUT_NOTIFY_DELAY_MS` notifies through the same service, by the `onUnanswered` callback of `requestPermissionFromUser`.

`reply/undo.ts` records the reply's turn (`reply/turns.ts`) once the run settles, so an edit landing after Stop belongs to the reply.

## An ACP reply

An ACP agent calls OpenPencil's tools through the MCP server, and its replies keep their edits the same way. The ACP transport (`transports/acp.ts`) starts a run for each reply with `startAgentRun`, without the built-in chat's agent presence, since the agent shows through its MCP session, and ends it however the reply ends. Each MCP tool call carries the chat id from the agent's `x-openpencil-chat` header and the call's id in the agent's conversation, which Codex sends as `_meta.callId` and Claude Code as `_meta["claudecode/toolUseId"]`. While the reply goes on, a call that edits the chat's own document joins the run through `runEditorTool`, which `automation/bridge/tool-handlers.ts` calls with the reply, so Revert, Restore, and the undone marks work as for a provider model.

Each request while the agent starts must answer within `AGENT_START_TIMEOUT_MS`, and Stop stops an agent that is still starting, so a message never waits on an agent that does not answer; either way the agent never gets the message.

## Undo and the model

A turn keeps the reply's calls and their undo entries. On every undo history change, each turn works out which of its calls are undone with `UndoManager.stateOf`: an entry on the redo stack is undone, one on the undo stack applied. An entry that left the history keeps its last state; undone and then cleared from Redo by a new edit, it stays undone. Changes are written to the reply's metadata, and the transcript reads only the metadata.

Edit → Undo and the chat's **Revert changes** therefore end in the same state: Revert undoes the reply's edits still applied, when they are the newest on the undo stack, and **Restore changes** redoes its undone edits, when Redo would bring exactly those back next.

`undoToReport` compares each reply's undone calls with what the model was last told, and the next message carries the difference as a note. The report records the message that carried it. If that message is sent again, for example when you edit it, the report is made again.

## Saved conversations

A reply's metadata (`chat/metadata.ts`) keeps whether you stopped it, and its edits with those undone and what the model was last told. Conversations save messages with `structuredClone`, so metadata is written from the plain message, never from the chat's reactive copy. Reopening a conversation settles any reply saved mid-way. The undo history does not survive closing a document, so a reopened reply keeps its marks but offers no Revert or Restore.

A reopened ACP or Pi conversation is read-only, since the conversation's context lives in the agent's own session, except with an agent whose `ACPAgentDef` sets `resumesSessions`: Claude Code and Codex. Once the agent starts answering a prompt, the ACP transport reports the agent's session id, since neither agent can resume a session that never took one, which the conversation saves as `agentSession`, and a later chat on the same agent continues it through ACP `session/resume` in the same agent workspace, without the instructions again and without replaying the transcript the chat already shows (`agents/acp/session.ts`, `chat/history/controller.ts`). A session the agent can no longer resume fails the message instead of starting a new session that would not know the conversation; the conversation forgets it, and the chat takes no more messages and shows as read-only. A conversation continued on another agent or model forgets its session too, and a session started on a conversation that already has messages is never saved, since it missed some of them.

## Compaction

A compaction is a message in the conversation (`chat/compaction/marker.ts`): a user message whose text is the summary and whose metadata marks it, so the transcript draws a divider and any backend that knows nothing of compaction still reads the summary. `messagesSinceCompaction` gives what a model reads, from the latest marker on; the tool loop sends only that. Undo notes still cover edits before it, which the summary describes as made. Saved conversations keep every message, so nothing changes in storage.

`chat/compaction/use.ts` runs it: the Design model summarizes the conversation (`summarize.ts`, with `prompt.md`), from a copy without images and with long tool results cut, so a conversation too long for its model can still be summarized; the marker is added only once the summary arrives, so a failed or cancelled compaction leaves the conversation as it was. One compaction runs at a time, and a message sent meanwhile waits for it. Before a message is sent, `compactIfFull` compacts when the last request since the latest marker, with the outgoing text estimated, passes `autoCompactAt` (`limits.ts`): the context window, from the model catalogs' `contextWindow`, less the whole reply allowance up to half the window, of which a tenth is kept for the next message. Compact and retry compacts only what came before the failed request, which stays after the summary to be asked again. Each reply keeps its token usage in its metadata (`usage`), written by the tool loop's `messageMetadata`, which the context meter and the reply's token line read. A provider error for a prompt past the window classifies as `context-limit`, whose notice offers Compact and retry.

Within one reply, `steps.ts` compacts between steps through the tool loop's `prepareStep`: when the last step's request passed the threshold, everything before that step's call and results becomes a summary of the model messages, and the step goes on from the summary and those. The reply records its compactions in its metadata as a list (`compactions`), each with the step it kept (`step`). The whole list is sent with each step's start, since a merge replaces it; `messagesSinceCompaction` then gives the summary and the reply from that step on, the reply draws the divider there, and `trace/rebuild.ts` rebuilds the later steps from the summary. Pi compacts its own context: `session.compact` in the harness protocol asks it to. `@ai-sdk/harness-pi` queues the `compaction` part of a compaction between turns and never delivers it. So once Pi confirms, the chat adds its own marker flagged `agent`, without a summary. `messagesSinceCompaction` skips that marker, and the Pi transport ignores manual reports. The compactions Pi runs on its own during a turn reach the reply as the same `compactions` metadata. ACP agents compact their own context.

## Traces

Save trace… in the conversation menu writes a file to reproduce what the agent did (`chat/trace/export.ts`). It holds the conversation's messages, its runs, and its diagnostic events.

A run is one message sent and every step the model took to answer it (`chat/trace/recorder.ts`). It records the model and settings, the last message sent, and per step the response's finish reason, usage, warnings, and duration; a failed run keeps the error, and the step that failed is the one after the last recorded. Instructions and the tools offered are stored once under their fingerprints and shared by every run that used them.

A step's request is not stored. It is the conversation through the run's last message, as `requestMessages` prepared it, plus the reply's earlier steps; `chat/trace/rebuild.ts` rebuilds it and compares its fingerprint with the one recorded when the step ran, so a rebuild that no longer matches what was sent is reported instead of replayed. Runs live in the chat database beside their conversation and are deleted with it.

---

---
url: 'https://openpencil.dev/development/behaviours-and-preview.md'
description: >-
  How components become working controls, how agents and scripts author them,
  and how preview runs them as live Reka UI islands.
---

# Behaviours and Preview

A behaviour makes a main component or component set work as a real control: a Switch, Slider, Tabs, Text field, and so on, after [Reka UI](https://reka-ui.com)'s primitives. It adds no node types. It describes which of the component's existing properties hold the control's values, which of its slots draw the control's parts, and which variants draw its interaction states. Preview then runs the control as the real Reka UI component, and code export can generate the same.

## The model

The model lives in `@open-pencil/scene-graph` (`packages/scene-graph/src/behaviours/`).

* **Kinds and contracts** (`kinds.ts`). `BEHAVIOUR_CONTRACTS` gives each kind its values and parts, keyed by kind, so a kind without a contract does not type-check. Contracts follow Reka UI's anatomy: every Reka subcomponent is a slot of the component, the component itself is the root, and a slot that holds repeated parts names the Reka part of its children, such as the tab list's triggers or a group's items.
* **Storage** (`schema.ts`, `model.ts`). A behaviour is stored as the `behaviour` field of OpenPencil's plugin data on the component or set, with properties and slots bound by id. Its role is `content`, so it travels with library assets and counts towards their update hash. `.fig` export renames the bound ids to the GUIDs it gives the properties.
* **Values**: a boolean is a variant property (with the values that mean on and off) or a boolean property; text is a text property; a number is the behaviour's own range, since Figma has no number property; a choice is which child of a slot is active.
* **States**: a variant property whose values draw rest, hover, pressed, focus, disabled, and, for a form control (`hasInvalidState`), invalid. `interactionStatesOf` lists the states a kind shows. Invalid is also a boolean value of form controls, for sets that draw it on a property of its own.
* **Specs** (`spec.ts`). `behaviourFromSpec` and `behaviourToSpec` convert between the stored behaviour and a spec that names properties and slots, which is how every authoring surface except the panel writes it. Errors name what the component has.

## Authoring surfaces

All of them write the same model.

| Surface | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Behaviour section | `src/components/properties/component-properties/behaviour/`, `useBehaviour` in `packages/vue` | Binds by id; Core's editor actions (`setBehaviour`, `addBehaviourText`, `addBehaviourVariant`, `addBehaviourPart`) create what is missing in one undo step. |
| `openpencil` scripting API | `packages/core/src/openpencil-api/` | The `openpencil` global next to `figma` in every script runner, through `compileScript`. |
| Tools | `packages/core/src/tools/create/behaviours.ts` | `set_behaviour`, `get_behaviour`, `create_slot`, built on the `openpencil` API. |
| Design JSX | `packages/design-jsx/src/behaviours/` | Reka-named elements (`Switch.Root`, `Switch.Thumb`) render and export components with behaviours. |

## Preview islands

Preview is a per-pane canvas view (`EditorViewState.canvasView`, `{ id: 'play', revision }`). It runs controls as real components; it never simulates them on the canvas. How the editor behaves in a view comes from its profile (`resolveEditorProfile` in `packages/core/src/editor/views/`): the pointer only pans, only shortcuts that switch or leave the view run, the canvas draws no editing chrome, a lone previewing pane hides the panels, and Escape returns to editing. Front ends read those values rather than the view's id.

1. **Islands.** `playIslandRoots` (Core) picks the top-level layers of the page that hold an instance with a behaviour. The renderer skips them while the pane previews, and `PlayIslands` (`packages/vue/src/canvas/islands/`) mounts one island per root, laid over the canvas at the pan and zoom of the canvas's last drawn frame, so the islands never run ahead of a canvas still catching up while panning and zooming.
2. **Shadow DOM.** Each island renders into its own shadow root: app CSS does not reach in, island CSS does not leak out, fonts already loaded by the app apply, and the island moves with the canvas in the same frame. Wheel gestures over an island are passed to the canvas.
3. **State to design.** An island keeps each control's state (values, choice, number, typed text, hover, pressed, focus). Core's `resolvePlayState` copies the island's layers into a private graph and shows each instance in its state: the matching variant, boolean properties, and layers a control reveals, such as tab panels. The copy comes from the page extractor history and export use (`extractPageContext`), with every variant of each instance's set so it can switch, and the document's variables and images shared rather than copied, since a state never changes them. The document is never changed.
4. **Design to DOM.** The private graph is projected to DOM through `@open-pencil/dom-css`, the same projection HTML export uses, so island fidelity and export fidelity improve together.
5. **DOM to Reka.** Each projected layer has a role: a control's root, a part, a group's item, a tab trigger or panel, or a text input. A tab list's triggers may be instances of a component with the `tab` behaviour: such a trigger keeps the trigger role and carries its own control, which the tabs turn on and off as a group turns its items, so its selected variant follows the choice, and which disables the trigger while it is drawn disabled. `behaviourControls` and `controlRoles` in `@open-pencil/dom-css` (`packages/dom-css/src/behaviours/`) assign them, so code export reads the same roles. Roles wrap the layer in its Reka UI primitive with `asChild`, so Reka renders through the designed element. Typing, focus, keyboard navigation, and accessibility are the browser's and Reka's.

Controls and DOM keys use layer paths (names below the island root), not node ids: a variant switch rebuilds an instance's layers with new ids, and a stable path keeps the DOM in place, including a focused input.

## Code export

Export reads the same model as preview. `behaviourArgs` gives a component set its props: a boolean value drawn by an on/off variant property becomes `checked`, `pressed`, `open`, `disabled`, or `invalid`. `invalid` sets `data-invalid` on the root and `aria-invalid` on the control a person fills in: a field's input, or else the root.

`stateStyles` merges a set's variants into one markup tree, matching layers by layer path:

* The rest variant is the base. Each other variant becomes a rule holding only what it changes, under conditions on the control's root.
* The conditions are the attributes Reka and Radix set, `data-state` and `data-disabled`; `data-invalid`, which the generated component sets from `invalid`; the browser's `:hover`, `:active`, and `:focus-visible`; and a `data-*` attribute for any other variant property, which the generated component sets from its prop. One states property shows one value at a time, so when it draws invalid, focus and the pointer leave an invalid control's look alone, and disabled wins over invalid; preview shows the states in the same order.
* Layers only some variants draw stay in the tree, hidden where absent, and a label that reads differently is a layer per state. A combination the set doesn't draw combines from its parts, and a drawn combination keeps only what its parts don't already give.

`stateStylesToCSS` writes the result as a stylesheet with a readable class per layer. `stateStylesToTailwind` writes it as utilities behind state variants, with a named group per control so a control nested in another reacts only to its own root.

## Adding a kind or a part

1. Add the kind to `BEHAVIOUR_KINDS` and its contract to `BEHAVIOUR_CONTRACTS` in scene-graph; part ids follow Reka's part names.
2. Map it in preview: its root and parts in `packages/vue/src/canvas/islands/controls/`, with the Reka primitives it uses.
3. Name its elements in design JSX: `REKA_ELEMENTS` in `packages/design-jsx/src/behaviours/index.ts` and the export's root table in `behaviours/export.ts`.
4. Label it in the Behaviour section (`labels.ts`) and translate the strings.
5. Cover the model and spec in scene-graph tests, preview in `tests/e2e/components/behaviours.spec.ts`, and JSX in `packages/core/tests/design-jsx/behaviours.test.ts`.

---

---
url: 'https://openpencil.dev/development/cloud.md'
---
# Cloud Architecture

OpenPencil Cloud is an optional, self-hostable backend for storing, sharing, and collaborating on
documents. The editor stays local-first: opening, editing, and saving local files never needs this
package, a network connection, or an account.

`@open-pencil/cloud` holds the network contracts, a typed client, a runtime-neutral Hono server, and
two runtimes that wire PostgreSQL, S3-compatible storage, email, and background work into it: a Node
process, and Cloudflare Workers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Editor[Editor and desktop app] -->|typed client| API[Hono server]
  API --> Auth[Better Auth sessions]
  API --> Policy[OpenFeature policy]
  API --> PG[(PostgreSQL metadata)]
  API -->|presigned URLs| S3[(S3-compatible objects)]
  Editor -->|presigned PUT and GET| S3
  Workers[Cleanup and email workers] --> PG
  Workers --> S3
  Workers --> SMTP[SMTP]
```

## Package boundaries

| Subpath                           | Contents                                                                   |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@open-pencil/cloud/contract`     | Valibot schemas and types shared by every side of the network              |
| `@open-pencil/cloud/client`       | Discovery, authentication, device authorization, and the typed Hono client |
| `@open-pencil/cloud/email`        | Vue Email rendering for transactional mail                                 |
| `@open-pencil/cloud/server`       | Hono routes and services; every dependency is injected                     |
| `@open-pencil/cloud/runtime/node` | PostgreSQL, S3, SMTP, the HTTP listener, workers, and operator commands    |

The Cloudflare runtime, `src/runtime/cloudflare`, isn't a subpath: Wrangler bundles it from
a deployment folder, type-checked against the Workers types by its own `tsconfig.json`.
`deploy/cloudflare` is the folder self-hosters copy; the official deployments are filled-in copies
under `deploy/openpencil/<target>`, which the Deploy Cloud workflow deploys with the secrets of the
`cloud-<target>` GitHub environment. A new target needs its folder, that environment, and an option
in the workflow.

The server never imports `pg`, opens a listener, runs migrations, or starts timers; runtimes do.
Browser code imports only `contract` and `client`, so it never pulls in server dependencies.

## Documents and revisions

PostgreSQL stores workspaces, membership, documents, revisions, uploads, sharing, and quota state.
Object storage stores immutable `.fig` revisions; a document points at its current revision, and every
revision has its own object key.

* Uploads go straight from the client to object storage through presigned single or multipart PUTs.
  The server verifies a SHA-256 digest before committing; ETags only complete multipart uploads.
* Each upload names the revision it was based on, so a stale base is rejected instead of silently
  overwriting a newer revision. The client then chooses: take the Cloud revision, keep both, or
  replace it.
* Deleting a document is immediate for users; the cleanup worker removes revisions and objects once
  the retention period passes.
* Images are stored once per workspace, keyed by the SHA-256 the object store verifies, and a stored
  revision leaves them out of its file: it lists the images it uses under the names the file gives
  them, and a download returns a link for each. Before a save the client asks which of its images
  the workspace lacks and uploads only those, each as an upload of its own kind with its own
  reservation, committed together in one request; asking renews the images the workspace holds.
  An image under a name Cloud does not accept stays inside the file. A save that names an image
  the workspace does not hold is refused. Keying by the verified checksum, with names kept per
  revision, means bytes uploaded under the wrong name can only reach the revision that named them.
* Restoring or duplicating a version gives the new revision the same images. Compaction releases an
  image no kept revision uses once a day has passed since a save last asked for it: its bytes return
  to the workspace's usage and the object sweep deletes its file.

### Version history

Every save is a revision, but the history a person sees is its versions: checkpoints the server
keeps on its own, and versions someone named (`document_version`, one per revision).

* When a save lands and the newest version is half an hour old, the server keeps the revision that
  save replaces as a checkpoint, so each stretch of editing and the state every session ended on stay
  in the history. A document's first save is always one.
* Naming the current state, or naming any version, makes it a named version; deleting its info turns
  it back into a checkpoint. Viewers see the history; editors name, restore, and duplicate.
* Restoring keeps the replaced state as a checkpoint, adds a revision that points at the restored
  version's stored file, and advances the collaboration epoch, so the live room starts over on it.
  Duplicating makes a new document in the same workspace from the same file. Neither uploads
  anything or uses more storage.
* A restore ends the document's rooms on the relay with close code `4410`, and the relay turns away
  tickets for an earlier epoch. A tab told so, or handed a ticket for another room, drops its queued
  uploads, shows the restored file it downloads, and joins the new room; a saver never overwrites a
  revision once its room has moved on.
* In the editor, File → Show version history makes the document read-only and lists its versions in
  the right sidebar, as Figma does. Choosing a version shows it in a read-only editor of its own in
  place of the document, whose room keeps syncing underneath; Save to version history (⌥⌘S) names
  the document once it is uploaded. A tab that does not save asks the room's saver on the `upload`
  channel, after its own edits, and names it when the saver answers that its upload finished. When
  a version is named, renamed, or turned back into an autosave, or a save adds a checkpoint, the
  server sends `versions` to the document's rooms and every open history loads it again; peers
  cannot send it.
* A document's address is `/documents/:id` on its server, with `?version=…` for a version; the
  editor keeps the address bar on the active tab's document and the version it shows when the
  document is on the server serving the editor, and a version's Copy link builds the address on the
  document's server. The address carries no secret: opening it signs in to the server at that
  address, one the app already knows or the official one, and the server's access rules decide. Fetching a version returns the version with its download, so
  a link can show it without paging the history.
* The cleanup worker compacts saves that are neither current nor a version once they are a day old,
  a batch at a time, and returns the bytes of files nothing else uses to the workspace's usage. A
  freed file's row stays until the object store deletes it, so a failed delete is retried. With
  the `revision_history` entitlement off, a workspace keeps 30 days of versions, as on a free plan.

## Authentication and authorization

Better Auth owns users, sessions, social sign-in, email and password, passkeys, TOTP, and recovery
codes. OpenPencil owns workspace and document authorization. For clients that cannot host a browser
redirect, such as the desktop app, the server supports the OAuth device authorization flow and
accepts the resulting bearer token.

Access to a document comes from ownership, workspace membership, a direct grant, or a capability
link, and the strongest source wins. Revoking one source leaves access inherited from another.
Documents granted to someone outside their own workspaces are listed for them separately, so a
client can show what was shared with them.

Workspace administrators invite people by email with a role. Workspace invitations use the same
`/invitations/:id` link as document invitations: preview and accept look for a workspace
invitation first and fall back to a document one, so email, the desktop handoff, and the editor's
invitation dialog serve both. A workspace with members always keeps an administrator.

Database rows use UUIDs. Capability secrets and invitation tokens are random hex; only their SHA-256
digests are stored, and they travel in URL fragments so they never reach access logs or `Referer`
headers. Invitation continuations through OAuth are single-use compact JWE.

Every sign-in is recorded in `sign_in` with the session it made and how it was made. A Better
Auth plugin, `accountActivity` in `src/server/auth/activity.ts`, reads the session an endpoint
issued from the hook context's `newSession`, which two-step sign-in leaves empty until the second
step, and the method from the endpoint, as Better Auth's own `lastLoginMethod` does: a password,
Google or Apple, a passkey, a second step, an email link, or the desktop app's device code. A person's Sessions page lists their live sessions with
that method and the browser the server reads from the user agent, and their latest sign-ins. A
sign-in from an address the account was never signed in from is emailed to its owner, except the
account's first. Adding or removing an authenticator app or a passkey is emailed too, and so is
an administrator resetting them.

A new email address is confirmed from that address through Better Auth's change-email link, and
the old address is told which address is taking over. An approved enrollment follows the account
to its new address, so the approval stays with the account.

Collaboration tickets are signed, epoch-scoped JWTs naming the principal and permission. Rotating a
capability secret keeps the current epoch; revoking access advances it so old tickets stop working.

## Live collaboration

Collaboration in the editor runs Yjs sync and awareness over a `CollabRoomTransport`. Local
documents use Trystero peer-to-peer; Cloud documents use the Cloud relay, a WebSocket endpoint at
`/api/collaboration/relay` on the API origin. Both carry the same room messages, so the editor has
one sync implementation.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Editor
  participant R as Relay (server peer)
  participant B as Viewer
  A->>R: auth (ticket)
  R-->>A: welcome [server]
  R->>A: sync-step1
  A->>R: sync-reply (offline edits)
  B->>R: auth (ticket)
  R-->>B: welcome [server, A]
  B->>R: sync-step1 to server
  R-->>B: sync-reply (room document)
  A->>R: yjs-update
  R-->>B: yjs-update
  B->>R: yjs-update (dropped)
```

The relay joins every room as a peer named `server`. It holds the room's Yjs document, saved by
document and collaboration epoch, so a newcomer gets the document even when nobody else is online.
A save logs what changed since the last one in PostgreSQL as a single update, a few bytes for a
typical edit, rather than rewriting the room; once the log reaches 500 updates or 4 MiB, and when
the room closes, a fresh snapshot replaces it. Snapshots are files in the object store beside the
documents' revisions, which a room's row names, so the database holds only the updates since the
last one. A compaction records its file before writing it and points the room at it last, so a
replaced or abandoned snapshot is one nothing refers to, which the object sweep removes once it is
15 minutes old. A room reopens from its snapshot and the updates logged after it. Tickets are
short-lived signed JWTs; the client presents a fresh one before the current one expires, and the
relay closes a socket whose ticket lapsed or changed identity. It checks a ticket when it hears from
the peer or sends it anything, not on a timer, so on Cloudflare an idle room's Durable Object
hibernates while its sockets stay open: each socket keeps its peer as an attachment, and the object
it wakes to resumes them and loads the room's document only once a message needs it. Presence alone
wakes the object without loading the document.

A socket message carries at most 256 KiB of a frame, under the deployment's per-message limit,
which may not be lower. A larger frame, such as a big paste, the first editor's copy of a large
document, or a newcomer's sync reply, travels as fragments in a row that the receiver joins again.
The relay joins an editor's fragments up to 256 MiB and holds viewers and peers not yet admitted to
one message, so only an editor can make it buffer more. A peer the relay turns away for good, for
a ticket, a full room, or a frame past those limits, leaves the room: the document's status says it
is not editing live and offers to rejoin, a viewer stays read-only, and an editor saves on its own,
since a tab that was not the room's saver had its edits counted as saved by the room.

Each runtime decides where rooms live. The Node process holds every room in one relay. On
Cloudflare, a Durable Object per document holds that document's rooms, and the Worker routes a
socket to it by the document named in the ticket's relay URL (`?document=`), since the ticket itself
arrives only after the upgrade; the object refuses tickets for any other document.

A Cloud room names its images instead of carrying them: an editor stores an image it adds in the
document's workspace and puts only its SHA-256 in the room's `imageRefs` map, and every peer loads
the images it lacks through links the server signs for anyone who may view the document, or for a
guest through its share link. A guest or a viewer cannot store images, so the ones it adds travel as
bytes until an editor in the room stores them and swaps them for references; a store that fails
leaves the bytes in the room. The room's state, which the relay saves, therefore holds no image
bytes once an editor has stored them. A peer that cannot load an image asks again later, waiting
longer each time up to a minute, while the room still names it.

The relay enforces what the ticket allows: a viewer's document updates and sync replies never leave
it, and presence updates are rewritten so others see the ticket's name and a `cloud` field with the
verified identity and permission. A peer cannot claim presence clients another peer owns. Voice is
not carried over the relay yet; the transport reports no media.

## Enrollment and administration

Enrollment is `open`, `approval`, or `closed`. In approval mode a verified identity creates a
pending request that a deployment administrator approves or rejects; approval can be revoked later.
Deployment administrators are separate from workspace administrators, and startup never grants
either role: the first operator is approved and promoted through the `admin` command.

The console's lists are tables the server pages, searches, and filters: each admin list endpoint
takes `search`, `filter`, `limit`, and `offset` and answers with its rows, the `total` matching, and
how many match the search under each filter (`src/admin/list.ts`). A list declares its filters once, as conditions on its table; one query counts them all with `count(*) filter (where …)`, and the page uses the same condition. People lists accounts in sign-up
order, searched by name or email and filtered to administrators, suspended accounts, or accounts
without two-step sign-in; access requests are searched by name or email in each status; email by
recipient and delivery; activity by the names of who acted and whom it was about, and by what it
was about. In the portal, `usePortalList` (`src/app/cloud-portal/list.ts`) holds a list's search,
filter, and page and builds its TanStack Table; `PortalTable` draws the toolbar, the shared
`AppDataTable`, and the pages, and each list only defines its columns, which render their cells with the components in `src/components/cloud-portal/table/`. A row has at most one inline
action, such as Approve; the rest are in its “…” menu. A person's page shows how they sign in, their workspaces, sessions, and recent
sign-ins. Administrators make and remove administrators, sign people out everywhere, suspend
with a reason the activity log keeps, and reset a locked-out person's two-step sign-in, which
removes their authenticator app, recovery codes, and passkeys, and take down a person's picture.
Every action asks once more.

Account pictures live in `user_picture`, one per account, and `user.image` holds the address the
server serves them from, `/api/pictures/:userId/:version`, where the version is the start of the
picture's SHA-256: a new picture is a new address. Responses are cached for one day, so a
picture an administrator removes may stay visible until the cache expires. The
page crops and shrinks a picture to a 256-pixel JPEG; the server accepts PNG or JPEG of at most
256 KB and 1024 pixels a side, reading the type and size from the bytes. A Google picture is
fetched when Better Auth writes the account's ID token, as it does when the account is linked and
at each sign-in with it, from the token's `picture` claim, and kept the same way unless the person
already shows a picture of their own; one that cannot be fetched leaves initials, never a link to
Google. The server fetches only from Google's picture host and follows no redirects. Nothing written
through Better Auth sets `user.image`; the server writes the addresses of the pictures it keeps
itself.

## Portal

The server shows its own pages on its public address: a welcome page, sign-in and sign-up, email
verification, password reset, two-step sign-in, desktop sign-in approval, account pages (profile,
sign-in and security, and sessions), and the administration console. They are a separate Vite entry, `cloud.html`, in the app project, so they
reuse the editor's components and theme without loading the editor. `bun run build:cloud` writes
them to `dist-cloud/` beside the editor itself, which every Cloud server serves at its root. The
editor never embeds these pages; when it needs them, for a social provider or a second sign-in
step, it opens them in a browser and gets the person back through `/auth/return` or the device
code. A verification link started in the editor lands on `/auth/verified`, which sends the person
back to the editor.

`CLOUD_PORTAL_PAGE_ROOTS` in the contract lists the page paths, and every runtime serves
`cloud.html` at and below them with `frame-ancestors 'none'`, so the approval page cannot be
framed. Both runtimes put the API behind the same Hono router, `createCloudServer` in
`src/runtime/site`, which answers portal pages before the API, and only where the API returns 404
the site's files, then the editor's `index.html` for any other page, so the editor's router keeps
its own addresses. Node reads the build named by `OPENPENCIL_CLOUD_SITE_DIR`, and the Worker reads
its static assets. `bun run cloud:dev` builds nothing: it runs Vite's development server for the
site under its own portless name and points the Node server at it with
`OPENPENCIL_CLOUD_DEV_SITE_URL`, so the server takes each file from source, uncached, and pages
update in place. Vite's update socket connects to its own address, since the server accepts
WebSockets only for collaboration.

The editor a server serves knows it from the build (`__OPENPENCIL_CLOUD_SITE__`). Before it boots,
it asks who is signed in: an account that may use the server gets the editor, and anyone else at
the root goes to `/welcome`, which signs them in, sends an account waiting for review to its
standing page, or opens the editor without an account; this browser then keeps that choice.
`[deployment] local_editor = false` takes that choice away and sends every editor page there.
Links to documents, shared files, and invitations always open the editor, which signs in for them,
and an unreachable server does too, since the editor works without it. The editor adds its server at startup and reaches it with the
server's own sign-in session, and the portal leaves for the editor as a page load, never through
its router. An official deployment builds the editor with its own address as
`VITE_OPENPENCIL_OFFICIAL_CLOUD_URL`, so staging is the official server in its own editor.

## Editor client

The editor treats each Cloud server as a profile of the `openpencil-cloud` storage provider, with a
workspace as the container, so the sync engine, recent files, and tabs handle Cloud documents the
way they handle a bucket. A server's id is hex from its address, which also names its credentials.
Email and password sign in inside the connect dialog wherever the server accepts the editor's
requests, which is the desktop app and the server's own editor address; the session's bearer token
goes in the credential store. Social providers and accounts with two-step sign-in finish in the
browser: the server's own editor address leaves for its pages and comes back, and the desktop app
approves a device code. Each connection tells a signed-in account from one waiting for approval, one
whose sign-in expired, and one never signed in.

Saves name the revision they were edited from, so a write over someone else's newer revision
becomes a conflict to resolve. Opening a Cloud document also joins its room on the relay. An empty
room takes the first editor's document once the relay has answered; a tab that opened the stored
file takes the room's copy when the room already has one, because each read of a `.fig` gives the
layers new IDs. One signed-in editor, the one with the lowest presence client, saves for the room;
the others drop their queued uploads and count their edits as saved. Guests who open a link join
the room with the link's permission and never save.

The room says what is unsaved, not the tab. Each peer counts its own edits to the room's document
under its Yjs client in the `edits` map, and the saver copies the counts its upload held into
`saved` once the server has that upload. What a tab takes from the room, including the replay when
it opens the stored file, is no edit of its own. The saver saves whenever any client has more edits
than `saved` records, so a tab that becomes the saver also saves edits an earlier saver left, and
opening a document nobody edited uploads nothing.

## Configuration

Operators author one schema-versioned TOML file. It owns URLs, trusted origins and proxies,
authentication providers, enrollment, object storage, email, worker schedules, retention,
entitlements, and technical limits, each in the section it limits. Environment variables only supply secrets, through references
such as `{ from_env = "DATABASE_URL" }`, and never override a value the file sets. TOML is parsed
with `smol-toml` and then validated and normalised by Valibot.

Technical limits are safety ceilings, not entitlements: runtime policy can be stricter but never
looser.

## Policy, entitlements, and quotas

OpenFeature answers concrete questions such as whether links work, whether guests, people who
follow a link without signing in, may view or edit through one, or whether full revision history
is kept, and what a numeric limit is. Links always work for people signed in to the server: the
share routes resolve the session, and a guest the server turns away gets `401` so the editor signs
in and opens the link again. Its provider reads one entitlement
source, chosen by `[entitlements] source`: the static table in the deployment TOML, which applies to
every workspace, or per-workspace rows in the database that the `entitlements` command sets. The two
are alternatives, not layers. Technical limits cap the file size and participant limits the source
reports.

Storage quota uses reservations: the upload locks the workspace's quota row, counts committed usage
plus active reservations, reserves the requested bytes, and commits the verified size when the
upload finishes. Cleanup releases reservations from abandoned uploads.

## AI service and billing

Cloud does not proxy models or keep credit balances. An `[ai]` table advertises a separate AI
service in discovery, and `POST /api/ai/token` signs a short-lived ES256 token for a workspace
member when the workspace has the `ai.enabled` entitlement. The token names the user, the
workspace, and its `ai.monthly_credit_allowance`; the service verifies it against the keys at
`/.well-known/jwks.json`, so it never reads Cloud's database. The contract editors and services
share, including the service's catalog, wallet, and error codes, is `src/contract/ai.ts`; it has its
own version so a service can change without a Cloud release. A `[billing]` table only advertises
where people manage their plan.

A service answers below its endpoint at the paths in `CLOUD_AI_API_PATHS`: model requests follow
the OpenAI chat completions API, so editors reach it with an OpenAI-compatible client, and the
catalog, wallet, and usage pages are the contract's own. The reference service is the AI relay in
`src/ai-relay`, run by `src/runtime/node/ai-relay`: it verifies tokens against Cloud's keys,
forwards completions to one upstream with one key, and keeps one usage row per settled request, so a
workspace's monthly spend is the sum of its rows. It reads usage from the upstream's answer, asking
streams for it with `stream_options.include_usage`, and keeps reading after the editor disconnects
so a request is still charged. It admits a request while credits remain and charges it afterwards,
so in-flight requests can overdraw an allowance; the official service reserves credits instead. An
answer ends only after its charge is recorded, so the wallet the editor reads once a reply ends
includes it, and a refusal for lack of credits says when the allowance renews. It forwards only
chat completion fields, so a router's fallback or provider fields cannot run a model outside the
catalog on its key. An upstream answer has ten minutes in all, streamed or not, before the relay ends it.

Services that decide entitlements, such as billing, write them through the internal API rather than
the database: `setWorkspaceEntitlements` in `src/server/internal`, which runtimes expose over HTTP
with a bearer token (`[internal_api]`) or a private transport of their own. Every write carries an
increasing `externalVersion`, and a write older than the stored one is refused, because billing
events arrive out of order. Cloud keeps answering from the last entitlements it received while the
writer is down.

## Rate limiting

OpenPencil routes use `hono-rate-limiter` with one PostgreSQL store that atomically increments
hashed, namespaced keys, so limits hold across instances. Better Auth keeps its own limiter for
`/api/auth/**`; those routes mount before OpenPencil middleware and are never counted twice.

## Transactional email

Vue Email renders matching HTML and plain-text bodies. Email goes through a PostgreSQL outbox: the
row is written in the same transaction as the change that caused it, payloads are encrypted at rest,
and a worker claims bounded batches with retries. The Node runtime sends through SMTP with
Nodemailer. On Cloudflare, Email Service sends what a request queued once the request finishes, and
a Cron Trigger retries the rest; `email.transport = "none"` disables delivery.

## Tests

| Level       | Location                                                      | Needs                   |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Unit        | `packages/cloud/tests/{client,contract,email,runtime,server}` | nothing                 |
| Integration | `packages/cloud/tests/integration`, mirroring `src`           | PGlite, in process      |
| End-to-end  | `packages/cloud/tests/e2e`                                    | Docker Compose services |

`bun run test:cloud` type-checks the package and runs unit and integration tests. The end-to-end
runners start PostgreSQL and SeaweedFS (or Garage) in an isolated Compose project, exercise presigned
and multipart uploads and the full revision flow, and remove the project afterwards. `test:e2e:cloudflare`
runs the Worker under `wrangler dev` against the same services and checks the API, the portal, and
the relay's Durable Object from outside.

## Decisions

Choices made while porting Cloud, with what was rejected and why. Add new entries at the end with
their date; revise an entry only by adding one that supersedes it.

**2026-10 · A relay instead of Hocuspocus.** The relay speaks the same room messages as Trystero, so
local and Cloud documents share one sync implementation. A Hocuspocus server would have needed a
second provider in the editor and its own authorization hooks for tickets and viewer filtering.

**2026-10 · The portal is a second Vite entry served only by the server.** Sign-in, approval, and
administration pages reuse the editor's components and theme without shipping in the editor
bundle, and a self-hosted server serves pages that match its own version. Pages inside the editor
would put the approval page under an origin the server does not control; a separate frontend
package would have duplicated the UI kit.

**2026-10 · Rooms are live whenever a Cloud document is open, and one editor saves.** Every open
tab joins the room, and the signed-in editor with the lowest presence client uploads for everyone,
so two people editing together never conflict with each other. Joining only on demand left
concurrent saves to the conflict dialog; building files on the server from the room's Yjs state
needs a headless `.fig` writer on the server, which is a later step.

**2026-10 · A tab takes the room's copy when the room has one.** Reading a `.fig` gives layers new
IDs, so two tabs that read the same file cannot merge their Yjs states. The first editor seeds an
empty room only after the relay answers, and later tabs adopt the room root.

**2026-10 · The room records what its revisions hold.** A tab compared with its own copy saw the
room's values as edits wherever a `.fig` round trip changes them, such as defaults it writes, so
every open uploaded a revision. Matching the round trip field by field breaks again with each new
field. Per-client edit counts in the room are what Yjs already merges, so no server change is
needed.

**2026-10 · Redirect sign-in only on the server's own editor address.** There the session cookie is
first-party and the server can send the person back to the same tab. The desktop app and editors on
other origins approve a device code instead of relying on third-party cookies or custom URL
schemes.

**2026-10 · Link secrets stay on the device that created them.** The server stores only digests,
like every capability secret, so a leaked database does not open documents. Other devices offer
**Reset link**, which rotates the secret, instead of a server that can hand the link back.

**2026-10 · Guests never save, and viewers are not locked yet.** A link opens a room with the link's
permission but no account to save under, so a signed-in editor saves for guests. The relay already
drops a viewer's document updates; locking the canvas for viewers needs a read-only mode in Core and
is a follow-up.

**2026-10 · Save to Cloud copies rather than moves.** The local file keeps its last saved contents
and the tab moves to the Cloud document, matching **Save to storage**. Moving would delete a file
the person may still open elsewhere.

**2026-10 · Home is split into places.** Recent files, each server's workspaces, documents shared
with the person, and the storage bucket are separate places in a sidebar, so Cloud does not crowd
the local file list and one server's workspaces show at a time.

**2026-10 · Cloud entry points wait for the official server's listing.** Settings → OpenPencil Cloud
and Save to Cloud stay hidden until `cloud.openpencil.dev` answers discovery with a `listing` whose
minimum editor version this editor meets, a server is already connected on the device, or someone
opened the editor with `?cloud=preview`. Launching, or pulling back, is a change to that server's
config rather than an editor release, and a launch that needs a client change sets the minimum to the
release that has it. A separate flags file or a third-party flag service would be one more thing to
deploy for one switch.

**2026-10 · Email and password sign in inside the editor.** The connect dialog signs in, signs up,
and waits for the verification link itself, and keeps a bearer token, so no cookie has to cross
from the server's address to the editor's; Safari treats sibling `.localhost` hosts as separate
sites and dropped that cookie. Signing in on the server's pages stays for social providers and the
second sign-in step, which need the server's own origin. This supersedes the redirect decision for
email and password.

**2026-10 · Settings → Cloud is always there.** Before the hosted service opens, its card holds the
waitlist, which used to sit under Storage, and a team's own server can be connected at any time.
This supersedes hiding Settings and Save to Cloud until the official server's listing.

**2026-10 · Every account starts with a workspace, and Save to asks only when there is a choice.**
An active account with no workspace gets one of its own when it first asks for its status, under a
slug fixed per person so concurrent requests make one. Save to goes straight to the only workspace
or bucket a document can go to, and New design creates in the place Home shows, so neither asks a
question with one answer. A setup step that makes people name a first workspace would stop them
before they have anything to put in it.

**2026-10 · Workspace invitations share the document invitation link.** Previewing an invitation
says whether it is for a document or a workspace, so one link format, one email path, and one
editor dialog cover both, and the desktop app's link handling needs no new kind. Invitation
continuations through OAuth stay document-only; the editor keeps a pending invitation itself.

**2026-10 · Cloud links hand off to the desktop app through `openpencil://cloud`.** Links stay web
addresses on the server's editor, so they work for anyone; the web editor on a computer offers the
desktop app, which gets the web link as `openpencil://cloud?url=<link>#<secret>`. The native side
checks the link, ID, and secret before the editor sees it. The secret is
visible in the launch arguments to other processes on the same computer; pasting links into the
app would avoid that at the cost of a manual step for everyone.

**2026-10 · Cloud's server is Apache-2.0, and the editor builds without it.** The server, relay,
administration, and the pages the server serves are Apache-2.0 for its patent grant; the protocol
in `contract` and `client` stays MIT, so the editor and other clients stay MIT. `REUSE.toml` maps
the paths rather than a separate package, which would have moved the protocol out of
`packages/cloud` for no legal gain. `VITE_OPENPENCIL_CLOUD=off` swaps Cloud's two entry points for
stand-ins, and `check:cloud-off` proves that build bundles none of Cloud.

**2026-10 · History is versions over revisions, compacted on the server.** Every save stays a
revision so saving and conflicts work as before, but the history lists only server-made checkpoints
and named versions, and saves between them are compacted after a day. Checkpoints are made when a
save lands rather than on a timer, so they need no client clock and cover every writer. History stores
`.fig` revisions rather than Yjs snapshots: snapshots would need garbage collection off in every room
and a version would still have to become a file to open, restore, or duplicate.

**2026-10 · AI services verify Cloud-signed tokens instead of calling Cloud.** A service checks a
token against a published key on every model request, with no round-trip to Cloud or its database,
and the same check serves the official service and self-hosted ones. Entitlements are read when a
token is signed, so a plan change reaches the service within one token lifetime; asking Cloud on
every request would have made model calls depend on Cloud's database. Entitlements are pushed to
Cloud rather than read from billing, so documents keep opening when billing is down.

**2026-10 · On Cloudflare, a Durable Object per document runs the relay.** The relay holds a room's
Yjs document and its peers in memory, which a stateless Worker can't, and keeping every epoch of a
document in one object lets a restore or a version change reach all its rooms in one call. Routing
needs the document before the ticket arrives, so the ticket's relay URL names it. Objects keep their
sockets without hibernation, so the relay runs unchanged; hibernating would need the relay to
rebuild rooms and peers on every wake.

**2026-10 · Every Cloud server serves the editor at its root.** The official web editor moves from
app.openpencil.dev to the official server's own address, so one site holds the editor, sign-in,
and documents, and a self-hosted server is a complete product too. On its own origin the editor
signs in through the server's pages and its session, with no device code and no CORS. A welcome
page meets visitors who are not signed in, and the editor stays usable without an account, as it
is on app.openpencil.dev, which can then redirect there. Keeping the editor only on a separate
static host left a signed-in person on account settings with no way to their files.

**2026-10 · Links name their server by their own address.** A document is `/documents/:id`, a
shared link `/share/:id`, and an invitation `/invitations/:id` on the server that holds them, with
no `server` parameter and no `/cloud` prefix, and the server has no separate editor address to
send them to. Peer-to-peer rooms move to `/rooms/:id` so "share" names a shared document. The
cost is that a browser editor at any other address cannot keep a Cloud document in its address
bar; every server serves its own editor, and the desktop app gets links through `openpencil://`.

**2026-10 · A link shows nothing until its document does.** A document link asks someone signed
out to sign in on the server's page before the editor loads, and comes back to the document. A
link that opens, or a sign-in the tab comes back from, keeps the boot splash's look over the
window until the document is drawn, over Home rather than an empty document, so a link that
fails or waits for a sign-in leaves the person on Home. A tab that holds its document never shows
the room's joining screen, since the room's state can arrive in parts. The cost is a longer
splash on a slow connection in place of an editor that fills in.

**2026-10 · Workspaces are deleted at once, not after a grace period.** GitLab keeps a deleted group
for 30 days so it can be restored; a Cloud workspace can only be deleted once it holds no
documents, and deleted documents already have their own retention, so a delay would protect
nothing but the name and members. Workspace settings stay in the editor's Members dialog, which
the desktop app reaches without leaving for a browser.

**2026-10 · Pictures are kept in the database, and Gravatar is not used.** A 256-pixel JPEG is
a few dozen kilobytes. Object storage only hands out short-lived signed links, so pictures there
would need upload tracking, a quota exemption, and a redirect for every picture a page shows; in a
table the server reads the bytes, checks them, and serves them itself. Gravatar would send every
viewer's address and a hash of each person's email to a third party, which a self-hosted server
should not do by default; copying a linked Google picture instead of linking to it follows the
same rule.

**2026-10 · Tables are named for what they hold.** OpenPencil's tables beside Better Auth's had a
`cloud_` prefix the rest never had; they lose it, and only a name Better Auth already uses gets a
qualifier (`api_rate_limit` beside its `rate_limit`). Migrations that shipped before the rename
type their queries against the names they ran with, so their SQL never changes.

---

---
url: 'https://openpencil.dev/development/navigation-performance.md'
---
# Navigation performance benchmark

The navigation benchmark measures the complete wheel/trackpad-to-render pipeline. It is intentionally separate from the synchronous microbenchmark in `tests/e2e/viewport/zoom-pan.spec.ts`: accepting JavaScript calls quickly does not prove smooth navigation.

## Renderer lifecycle and ownership

The benchmark validates the tiled renderer contracts documented in [Renderer lifecycle and ownership](./renderer-lifecycle.md). Structural renderer changes must preserve those generation, settlement, and CanvasKit ownership rules.

## What it captures

Every run writes `recording.json`, `metrics.json`, and `environment.json`. When tracing is enabled, it also writes `trace.json.gz`:

* `trace.json.gz` (when tracing is enabled): Chromium tracing data for Perfetto or Chrome tracing tools.
* `recording.json`: wheel samples plus OpenPencil input, viewport, render, and tile coverage events.
* `metrics.json`: frame pacing, input latency, zoom-anchor drift, viewport jumps, exact active-renderer settlement, and tiled scheduler throughput/cancellation when enabled.
* `environment.json`: browser, runtime, replay mode, and source gesture information.

OpenPencil emits User Timing marks under `openpencil:*`, including wheel receipt/flush, viewport mutation, render start/end, and exact tiled coverage. The recording also runs a continuous `requestAnimationFrame` heartbeat and observes browser Long Tasks, so display stalls remain visible even when OpenPencil does not render.

## Record a physical macOS trackpad gesture

1. Start a production preview (preferred) or development server:

   ```sh
   bun run build
   bun run preview -- --port 1420
   ```

2. Open:

   ```text
   http://localhost:1420/?test&no-chrome&no-rulers&navigation-benchmark
   ```

3. In DevTools, start recording:

   ```js
   openPencil.test.navigation.startRecording('macbook-fast-pinch-reversal')
   ```

4. Perform exactly one gesture, allow the canvas to become crisp, then stop and copy the result:

   ```js
   copy(JSON.stringify(openPencil.test.navigation.stopRecording(), null, 2))
   ```

5. Save the result under `tests/fixtures/navigation/gestures/`. Do not edit delta values or timestamps. Remove document names if they contain private information.

Record at least slow pan, momentum pan, direction reversal, slow pinch, fast pinch in/out, pinch reversal, diagonal pan, and the personally observed failing gesture. Recordings from actual hardware must use `source: "macos-trackpad"`; generated fixtures use `source: "synthetic"`.

## Benchmark a real `.fig` fixture

Use `current-document` with an explicit browser-served fixture path. The runner waits for loading and page population, applies layout through the normal document-open path, zooms to fit, and waits on the active renderer's explicit settlement contract before recording:

```sh
bun run benchmark:navigation \
  --url http://localhost:1420/ \
  --gesture tests/fixtures/navigation/gestures/synthetic-pinch-reversal.json \
  --mode dom \
  --scenario current-document \
  --document tests/fixtures/gold-preview.fig \
  --no-trace \
  --output artifacts/navigation-benchmark/gold-preview
```

`environment.json` records the resolved local document path so reports cannot silently mix generated and real-document runs. The runner serves the exact local bytes through an isolated Playwright route, so production Vite preview does not return its SPA fallback for non-public test fixtures.

## Replay with Chromium tracing

```sh
bun run benchmark:navigation \
  --url http://localhost:1420/ \
  --gesture tests/fixtures/navigation/gestures/synthetic-pinch-reversal.json \
  --mode cdp \
  --scenario raster-stress \
  --output artifacts/navigation-benchmark/current
```

`--mode cdp` sends browser input through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. `--mode dom` deterministically dispatches events inside the page and is useful for scheduler/correctness debugging. Neither mode is represented as physical WKWebView input.

Use `--no-trace` for the lowest-overhead metrics pass. Run a separate diagnostic pass with tracing enabled, and add `--cpu-profile` only when stack sampling is needed: CPU profiling can perturb the timing being measured.

Performance runs require a hardware-accelerated Metal/ANGLE context and fail if Chromium falls back to SwiftShader. Use `--software-gpu` only for portable correctness and CI smoke runs; never compare its timings with hardware results. Every run records the unmasked GL renderer and vendor in `environment.json`.

Open the trace:

```sh
open https://ui.perfetto.dev
```

Then load `trace.json.gz` and search for `openpencil:`.

## Baseline comparison

Build and run the same gesture against `v0.14.0` and the candidate in separate clean worktrees, on the same machine and power state. Alternate baseline/candidate runs rather than completing every baseline run first. Use release builds, fixed 1280×800 CSS viewport and DPR 2, and at least five measured repetitions after one warmup.

Do not gate shared CI on absolute timing. Dedicated benchmark hardware may gate on same-run baseline ratios and correctness invariants. Always retain raw traces for regressions.

Compare two completed runs:

```sh
bun tools/dev/navigation-benchmark/src/cli.ts compare \
  --baseline artifacts/navigation-benchmark/v0.14.0/metrics.json \
  --candidate artifacts/navigation-benchmark/current/metrics.json \
  --output artifacts/navigation-benchmark/comparison.json
```

## Metrics

The report includes:

* Frame interval median, p95, p99, maximum, and counts over 8.33/16.67/33.33/50 ms.
* Render CPU interval and CanvasKit flush timing.
* Wheel-to-viewport and wheel-to-render-end latency.
* Maximum zoom focal-point drift in screen pixels.
* Maximum presented viewport displacement between rendered frames.
* Final input to exact visible tile coverage, the renderer's settlement.
* Tiled scheduler frame count, maximum jobs per frame, maximum measured job submission, over-budget jobs, deadline overrun, and cancelled obsolete jobs.

The runner contains no warmup or settlement sleeps. `waitForSettlement()` requires an idle navigation lifecycle and renderer-owned exact coverage; its timeout rejects the benchmark and reports renderer state.

### Benchmark content mutation and cancellation

Use the exact imported node ID plus a deterministic property mutation to measure selective refresh:

```sh
bun run benchmark:navigation \
  --url 'http://localhost:1420/' \
  --gesture tests/fixtures/navigation/gestures/synthetic-repeated-pinch-reversal.json \
  --mode dom \
  --scenario current-document \
  --document tests/fixtures/gold-preview.fig \
  --mutate-node '0:5' \
  --mutate-opacity 0.11 \
  --no-trace \
  --output artifacts/navigation-benchmark/gold-preview-mutation
```

Add `--replay-after-mutation` to wait until refresh is observably pending and then replay the gesture before exact settlement. This measures generation cancellation and final-viewport prioritization without a fixed delay.

Mutation-only and combined runs record their mutation parameters in `environment.json`. For tiled runs, inspect `scheduler.cancelledJobs`, `maximumJobsPerFrame`, `maximumJobRenderMs`, `overBudgetJobs`, and `maximumDeadlineOverrunMs`.

Averages alone are not acceptance criteria. Inspect p95/p99, maximum stalls, contiguous missed frames, motion discontinuities, and crisp-settlement latency.

## Required fixture matrix

Permanent benchmark scenarios should cover:

* **Light:** isolates input and scheduling overhead.
* **Large flat:** stresses culling and traversal.
* **Realistic:** nested frames, text, images, gradients, effects, masks, and instances.
* **Raster stress:** expensive tile rendering and coverage changes.
* **Imported `.fig`:** exercises imported-document rendering paths.

Keep large or binary `.fig` fixtures in Git LFS. Synthetic fixture generation must be deterministic.

## Native macOS acceptance

Chromium replay does not establish WKWebView or physical trackpad behavior. Before a release with navigation changes:

1. Build a release-mode Tauri application.
2. Record the same gesture on physical target hardware.
3. Capture Instruments **Time Profiler** and **Core Animation** traces, including OpenPencil and WebKit processes.
4. Check input delivery, main-thread/WASM work, GPU/compositor stalls, viewport continuity, and final crisp settlement.
5. Store the recording, metrics, hardware/macOS metadata, and Instruments trace as release artifacts.

Native automation may add OS-level scroll injection, but it must preserve continuous-scroll and momentum phases before being called trackpad-equivalent. Synthetic composition or DOM wheel events are not native acceptance evidence.

---

---
url: 'https://openpencil.dev/development/renderer-lifecycle.md'
---
# Renderer lifecycle and ownership

The CanvasKit renderer keeps hot drawing loops direct, but its tiled path follows explicit lifecycle contracts. Preserve these contracts when changing renderer structure or cache policy.

## Navigation and settlement

The scene layer renders through tiles; only a canvas that owns the whole frame, such as a thumbnail or an export, draws the scene as one picture. Tiles render at the exact device scale and are presented on whole device pixels, so a settled view is never resampled. It presents cached tiles whether or not navigation is active, covers a missing tile with the cached tiles of the nearest level scaled into place, and leaves areas no level covers at the page colour until their tiles render; it never draws the whole-scene picture, which a large document cannot afford. Panning keeps rasterizing under a smaller frame budget and runs at most one tile estimated past it; a zoom whose level moves renders, under that budget, the quantized step at or above the scale, whose tiles serve until the zoom crosses the next step and then stand in for the exact level scaled by a fifth at most, over the pyramid, the page copy, and the earlier levels; a zoom that pauses renders the exact level under the moving budget; a level is presented only once every visible tile of it exists, the nearest level standing in whole until then, or the page colour when the page is first shown, so a zoom or a page open ends with the viewport appearing in one frame, while a level once presented shows the tiles a pan reveals or an edit renews as they land; the background stages wait until the content has been still for 300 ms, so an edit in progress rebuilds the visible tiles alone and the coarse copies under it once it pauses; a tile whose chunk pictures are not all recorded records them until the frame's budget is spent and defers the rest; queued jobs for another level or an earlier navigation generation are discarded. Idle time builds, in order, the whole page at a level where it spans four tiles, the overscan ring, a pyramid of levels each downsampled from the four cached tiles twice as fine, and a scene-rendered backdrop four times coarser around the viewport, so a hole anywhere over the page finds a scaled stand-in; a missing tile draws the nearest level that covers its overlap with the page fully, found past any partial levels, with up to two nearer partial levels layered on top; the page copy is kept most recently used, so it is evicted last. A tile not rendered yet is estimated from its chunk count at the per-chunk time measured for its level, or for any level until its own is known. The tile cache's byte budget follows the viewport, five viewports of tiles between 128 MB and 768 MB, and a frame of background work that evicts a tile of its own plan's levels stops the background stages until the level or the viewport changes, so a cache too small for the plan holds what it has rather than rendering in circles. A layer added, removed, moved, or changed in kind rebuilds only the chunks of the smallest subtree that held it, slotted into the draw order between their neighbours, and drops the pictures and tiles those chunks touched; the page's own children added, removed, or reordered renumber the draw order of all chunks, and only a document loaded or replaced rebuilds the index from nothing. The controller reports background work separately from visible work: settlement waits only for the visible tiles, while the frame loop keeps idle frames coming until the background stages are built. A tile over nothing holds no texture. Fonts arriving redraw only the text that waited for them. Visible exact coverage while idle is the settlement boundary; overscan remains background work.

Generation rules:

* Navigation generations cancel obsolete queued tile work.
* Content generations invalidate affected pictures and tiles.
* Page, scene, position-preview, and font versions all participate in picture and tile validity.
* A stale build or raster result must be deleted rather than installed.

## CanvasKit ownership

CanvasKit objects are native/WASM resources and are not reclaimed reliably by JavaScript garbage collection. Ownership transfer must remain explicit.

| Resource | Created by | Owner after success | Released by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whole-scene picture | Scene recorder | `wholeScene` | Replacement, invalidation, renderer destruction |
| Node picture | Node picture recorder | `nodePictures` | Node invalidation, font generation change, renderer destruction |
| Chunk picture | Chunk recorder | `RenderChunkPictureCache` | Chunk invalidation or cache clear |
| Tile image | `renderTile()` | Caller until installation, then `TileImageCache` | Stale-result discard, replacement, eviction, cache clear |
| Tile surface | `TileSurfacePool` | Surface pool | Pool clear |
| CanvasKit path arrays | Geometry builder | Owning geometry cache | Node invalidation or renderer destruction |

Do not introduce generic disposal wrappers into per-node or per-tile hot loops. Prefer narrow domain operations with obvious transfer points, and use `try/finally` around recorder, surface, paint-effect, and transform lifetimes.

## Performance-preserving refactors

Safe structural refactors may split modules, name state records, extract telemetry, and document transitions. They must not change:

* Frame budgets, cache limits, tile size, quantized levels, or overscan policy.
* Visible-before-overscan priority.
* Direct CanvasKit calls and preallocated temporary buffers in hot loops.
* Atomic isolation for masks, opacity, blend modes, and blur scopes.
* Exact settlement acknowledgement.

Validate structural changes with the `gold-preview.fig` reversal and mutation-plus-reversal benchmarks, focused renderer tests, and committed canvas snapshots. Compare production builds rather than relying on synchronous microbenchmarks.
